newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss deny secret deals on Jewish funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss deny secret deals on Jewish funds.

text.p: Switzerland on Thursday denied a U.S. senator's assertion it had struck secret deals that let it tap the unclaimed wealth of Eastern European Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for property nationalised by communist regimes.

But it pledged to review any evidence that Alfonse D'Amato, whose Senate Banking Committee is probing the fate of Jewish wealth left in Swiss banks by Holocaust victims, could provide to shed more light on Switzerland's wartime history.

At a hearing in New York on Wednesday, D'Amato said researchers had found documents showing the Swiss struck just such a secret deal in 1949 with Poland and subsequently with Hungary and Czechoslavakia.

"We had agreements with all countries after the war. None of those is secret. Our archives are open and none are related to the subject Mr D'Amato was speaking about yesterday," Swiss foreign ministry spokesman Jean-Philippe Tissieres told Reuters.
The 1949 accord with Poland, for example, calls for Warsaw to pay Switzerland 52.1 million Swiss francs for Swiss property it seized, but does not mention Jewish accounts in Switzerland.

Tissieres said Switzerland welcomed any new contributions D'Amato could make to its historical review. These would be checked in the spirit of the government's determination "to shed all light on the matter."

Swiss bankers demanded more time to probe fresh accusations raised at the New York hearing that they deliberately stonewalled families of Holocaust victims who had deposited wealth in Switzerland before the Nazis exterminated them.
The Swiss Bankers Association (SBV) insisted banks and officials were doing their utmost to clear up the claims that have drawn international attention.
"We have already started and now it is a matter of letting us get down to work," said SBV spokeswoman Sylvia Matile.
At the hearing, Holocaust survivors wept while recalling their ordeal trying to persuade Swiss banks to hand back murdered relatives' wealth.
One woman, Estelle Sapir, bitterly recalled how some banks refused her access to family accounts unless she produced a death certificate for her father, who died in a Nazi death camp.
Credit Suisse, one of the banks Sapir mentioned, said it was sorry if it in fact treated her in such a way.

"If this happened then we are certainly very sorry, but we are not able to verify this after 50 years," a bank spokeswoman said, but she added Swiss banking secrecy prevented her from either confirming or denying the incident ever took place.
"I can guarantee you that our customers would not be handled this way today," she said.
The Swiss banking ombudsman in charge of helping nearly 1,000 claimants track down lost Holocaust accounts, Hanspeter Haeni, agreed such a thing would never happen again now.

"We want to prevent people from asking for information to which they are not legitimately entitled, so we need some information, but of course we have cases from the war with Holocaust victims where documents can't be produced and in these cases we try in an individual way to do without," he said.

A separate panel agreed by Swiss bankers and Jewish groups in May and headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker is also checking if banks did all they could to locate Holocaust victims' accounts. It meets in Zurich on Friday.

In addition, parliament is set to agree in December the formation of a panel of experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a sweeping five-year review of Swiss financial links to the Nazis and review the fate of Nazi victims' wealth.
